exam: A 6‑year‑old with multiple café‑au‑lait spots and recent gait disturbance – what is the next diagnostic step and why? — Assess for optic pathway glioma with fundus exam; MRI if available to rule out intracranial tumours.

How would you differentiate NF1 from Sturge‑Weber in a child with facial rash? — Look for port‑wine stain in V1 distribution and leptomeningeal calcifications (Sturge‑Weber) versus café‑au‑lait macules and axillary freckling (NF1).
A child with TSC presents with worsening seizures; why might you avoid carbamazepine? — Carbamazepine induces CYP enzymes, reducing everolimus levels used for tumour control.
What red‑flag sign in a neurocutaneous patient mandates urgent neuro‑imaging? — Acute hydrocephalus signs (headache, vomiting, papilledema).

Explain why routine blood tests are often normal in neurocutaneous syndromes despite severe disease. — The primary pathology is structural/genetic, not metabolic; labs may only show secondary effects.
In a low‑resource setting without MRI, how would you monitor for subependymal giant cell tumour growth? — Serial head circumference, neurological exam, and fundoscopic assessment for papilledema.
Why is genetic counselling essential for families with NF1? — Autosomal dominant inheritance gives a 50 % risk to offspring; counselling guides family planning.
What is the most important preventive measure for malignant transformation of neurofibromas? — Early surgical removal of rapidly enlarging or painful lesions and regular surveillance.
ai.title: Neurocutaneous Syndromes
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Neurocutaneous syndromes are hereditary disorders that affect skin, nervous system and sometimes other organs. Recognising the pattern of skin lesions with neurological signs guides diagnosis, especially where advanced testing is limited.

b: Diagnosis is clinical: skin stigmata + neurological findings
Confirm with targeted genetic testing when available
sections.p: A group of genetic conditions that produce characteristic cutaneous lesions together with central or peripheral nervous system abnormalities.

b: Mild – isolated skin lesions, normal development
Moderate – seizures, focal neurological deficits, visual loss
Severe – progressive neurodegeneration, hydrocephalus, malignant tumours
sections.p: Severity is organ‑specific; most centres use a functional staging (mild, moderate, severe) based on neurological disability and extent of systemic involvement.

b: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) – NF1 gene mutation
Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) – TSC1/TSC2 mutation
Sturge‑Weber syndrome – GNAQ somatic mutation
Hypomelanosis of Ito – mosaic chromosomal abnormalities
Rare: von Hippel‑Lindau, Cowden, Incontinentia pigmenti
sections.p: Most are autosomal dominant mutations affecting the RAS‑MAPK pathway or tumor‑suppressor genes.

b: Café‑au‑lait macules, axillary freckling (NF1)
Facial angiofibromas, ash‑leaf spots, shagreen patches (TSC)
Port‑wine stain over the face, leptomeningeal calcifications (Sturge‑Weber)
Seizures, developmental delay, focal deficits, visual field loss
sections.p: Children present with skin findings that precede or accompany neurological signs.

t.b: Confirms pigmentary lesions; helps differentiate hypomelanosis of Ito from other macules
Detects cortical tubers, subependymal nodules, leptomeningeal angiomas; guides neurosurgical referral
Looks for optic pathway glioma (NF1) or retinal hamartomas (TSC)
Provides definitive diagnosis; if unavailable, rely on clinical criteria
Identifies epileptiform activity; helps plan antiepileptic therapy

b: Rapidly enlarging neurofibroma → suspect malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour
Acute hydrocephalus from obstructive lesions (TSC, Sturge‑Weber)
Severe, refractory seizures
Progressive visual loss from optic glioma
sections.p: Complications can be life‑threatening and need urgent attention.

b: Surgical excision of symptomatic neurofibromas or vascular malformations
mTOR inhibitors (e.g., everolimus) for growing subependymal giant cell tumours in TSC – chosen for tumour control, avoid steroids that raise infection risk
Antiepileptic drugs for seizures – avoid enzyme‑inducing agents if on mTOR inhibitors
Regular ophthalmology review – early laser or surgery for optic glioma
Physiotherapy and developmental support
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, control symptoms and monitor for complications.

b: Annual skin exam, neuro exam and blood pressure check
MRI every 2–3 years in high‑risk patients (if affordable)
Vaccinate against varicella and HPV – reduces tumour‑related complications
Counselling on avoiding trauma to neurofibromas
sections.p: Lifelong surveillance is essential because new lesions and complications can appear at any age.

b: Neurofibromatosis type 2 – bilateral vestibular schwannomas, no café‑au‑lait
Congenital melanocytic nevus – large pigmented patch without neurological signs
Meningitis – can cause seizures and rash but lacks chronic skin stigmata
Normal MRI does not exclude early cortical tubers; rely on clinical skin criteria
Negative genetic test does not rule out mosaic disorders – clinical diagnosis remains paramount
